entries.47a07e1905c75cca40d2a96c2cac6ef4dc758f7c: <div sID="gen9622" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Job.16" sID="Job.16"/> <div eID="gen9622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9623" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9624" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins Job's reply to that discourse of Eliphaz which we had in the foregoing chapter; it is but the second part of the same song of lamentation with which he had before bemoaned himself, and is set to the same melancholy tune. I. He upbraids his friends with their unkind usage of him, <reference osisRef="Job.16.1-Job.16.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. He represents his own case as very deplorable upon all accounts, <reference osisRef="Job.16.6-Job.16.16">ver. 6-16</reference>. III. He still holds fast his integrity, concerning which he appeals to God's righteous judgment from the unrighteous censures of his friends, <reference osisRef="Job.16.14-Job.16.22">ver. 14-22</reference>.
entries.feb6e403d90406c9edfe33ffec203f6242839a73: <div eID="gen9624" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9623" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Reply of Job to Eliphaz. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9625" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Job answered and said, <hi type="super">2</hi> I have heard many such things: miserable comforters <hi type="italic">are</hi> ye all. 3 Shall vain words have an end? or what emboldeneth thee that thou answerest? <hi type="super">4</hi> I also could speak as ye <hi type="italic">do:</hi> if your soul were in my soul's stead, I could heap up words against you, and shake mine head at you. <hi type="super">5</hi> <hi type="italic">But</hi> I would strengthen you with my mouth, and the moving of my lips should assuage <hi type="italic">your grief.</hi> <div eID="gen9625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9626" type="x-p"/> Both Job and his friends took the same way that disputants commonly take, which is to undervalue one another's sense, and wisdom, and management. The longer the saw of contention is drawn the hotter it grows; and the <hi type="italic">beginning of</hi> this sort of <hi type="italic">strife is as the letting forth of water; therefore leave it off before it be meddled with.</hi> Eliphaz had represented Job's discourses as idle, and unprofitable, and nothing to the purpose; and Job here gives his the same character. Those who are free in passing such censures must expect to have them retorted; it is easy, it is endless: but <hi type="italic">cui bono?—what good does it do?</hi> It will stir up men's passions, but will never convince their judgments, nor set truth in a clear light. Job here reproves Eliphaz, 1. For needless repetitions (<reference osisRef="Job.16.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have heard many such things.</hi> You tell me nothing but what I knew before, nothing but what you yourselves have before said; you offer nothing new; it is the same thing over and over again." This Job thinks as great a trial of his patience as almost any of his troubles. The inculcating of the same things thus by an adversary is indeed provoking and nauseous, but by a teacher it is often necessary, and must not be grievous to the learner, to whom <hi type="italic">precept must be upon precept, and line upon line.</hi> Many things we have heard which it is good for us to hear again, that we may understand and remember them better, and be more affected with them and influenced by them. 2. For unskilful applications. They came with a design to comfort him, but they went about it very awkwardly, and, when they touched Job's case, quite mistook it: "<hi type="italic">Miserable comforters are you all,</hi> who, instead of offering any thing to alleviate the affliction, add affliction to it, and make it yet more grievous." The patient's case is sad indeed when his medicines are poisons and his physicians his worst disease. What Job says here of his friends is true of all creatures, in comparison with God, and, one time or other, we shall be made to see it and own it, that miserable comforters are they all. When we are under convictions of sin, terrors of conscience, and the arrests of death, it is only the blessed Spirit that can comfort effectually; all others, without him, do it miserably, and sing songs to a heavy heart, to no purpose. 3. For endless impertinence. Job wishes that <hi type="italic">vain words might have an end,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.16.3">v. 3</reference>. If vain, it were well that they were never begun, and the sooner they are ended the better. Those who are so wise as to speak to the purpose will be so wise as to know when they have said enough of a thing and when it is time to break off. 4. For causeless obstinacy. <hi type="italic">What emboldeneth thee, that thou answerest?</hi> It is a great piece of confidence, and unaccountable, to charge men with those crimes which we cannot prove upon them, to pass a judgment on men's spiritual state upon the view of their outward condition, and to re-advance those objections which have been again and again answered, as Eliphaz did. 5. For the violation of the sacred laws of friendship, doing by his brother as he would not have been done by and as his brother would not have done by him. This is a cutting reproof, and very affecting, <reference osisRef="Job.16.4-Job.16.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. (1.) He desires his friends, in imagination, for a little while, to change conditions with him, to put their souls in his soul's stead, to suppose themselves in misery like him and him at ease like them. This was no absurd or foreign supposition, but what might quickly become true in fact. So strange, so sudden, frequently, are the vicissitudes of human affairs, and such the turns of the wheel, that the spokes soon change places. Whatever our brethren's sorrows are, we ought by sympathy to make them our own, because we know not how soon they may be so. (2.) He represents the unkindness of their conduct towards him, by showing what he could do to them if they were in his condition: <hi type="italic">I could speak as you do.</hi> It is an easy thing to trample upon those that are down, and to find fault with what those say that are in extremity of pain and affliction: "<hi type="italic">I could heap up words against you,</hi> as you do against me; and how would you like it? how would you bear it?" (3.) He shows them what they should do, by telling them what in that case he would do (<reference osisRef="Job.16.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">"I would strengthen you,</hi> and say all I could to assuage your grief, but nothing to aggravate it." It is natural to sufferers to think what they would do if the tables were turned. But perhaps our hearts may deceive us; we know not what we should do. We find it easier to discern the reasonableness and importance of a command when we have occasion to claim the benefit of it than when we have occasion to do the duty of it. See what is the duty we owe to our brethren in their affliction. [1.] We should say and do all we can to strengthen them, suggesting to them such considerations as are proper to encourage their confidence in God and to support their sinking spirits. Faith and patience are the strength of the afflicted; whatever helps these graces confirms the feeble knees. [2.] To assuage their grief—the causes of their grief, if possible, or at least their resentment of those causes. Good words cost nothing; but they may be of good service to those that are in sorrow, not only as it is some comfort to them to see their friends concerned for them, but as they may be so reminded of that which, through the prevalency of grief, was forgotten. Though hard words (we say) break no bones, yet kind words may help to make broken bones rejoice; and those have the <hi type="italic">tongue of the learned</hi> that know how to <hi type="italic">speak a word in season to the weary.</hi>
entries.37a15d15f3feffcf9a40761f1cfc79fa11cfe45c: <div eID="gen9626" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Grievances of Job. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9627" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Though I speak, my grief is not assuaged: and <hi type="italic">though</hi> I forbear, what am I eased? <hi type="super">7</hi> But now he hath made me weary: thou hast made desolate all my company. <hi type="super">8</hi> And thou hast filled me with wrinkles, <hi type="italic">which</hi> is a witness <hi type="italic">against me:</hi> and my leanness rising up in me beareth witness to my face. <hi type="super">9</hi> He teareth <hi type="italic">me</hi> in his wrath, who hateth me: he gnasheth upon me with his teeth; mine enemy sharpeneth his eyes upon me. <hi type="super">10</hi> They have gaped upon me with their mouth; they have smitten me upon the cheek reproachfully; they have gathered themselves together against me. <hi type="super">11</hi> God hath delivered me to the ungodly, and turned me over into the hands of the wicked. <hi type="super">12</hi> I was at ease, but he hath broken me asunder: he hath also taken <hi type="italic">me</hi> by my neck, and shaken me to pieces, and set me up for his mark. <hi type="super">13</hi> His archers compass me round about, he cleaveth my reins asunder, and doth not spare; he poureth out my gall upon the ground. <hi type="super">14</hi> He breaketh me with breach upon breach, he runneth upon me like a giant. <hi type="super">15</hi> I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin, and defiled my horn in the dust. 16 My face is foul with weeping, and on my eyelids <hi type="italic">is</hi> the shadow of death; <div eID="gen9627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9628" type="x-p"/> Job's complaint is here as bitter as any where in all his discourses, and he is at a stand whether to smother it or to give it vent. Sometimes the one and sometimes the other is a relief to the afflicted, according as the temper or the circumstances are; but Job found help by neither, <reference osisRef="Job.16.6">v. 6</reference>. 1. Sometimes giving vent to grief gives ease; but, "<hi type="italic">Though I speak</hi>" (says Job), "<hi type="italic">my grief is not assuaged,</hi> my spirit is never the lighter for the pouring out of my complaint; nay, what I speak is so misconstrued as to be turned to the aggravation of my grief." 2. At other times keeping silence makes the trouble the easier and the sooner forgotten; but (says Job) <hi type="italic">though I forbear</hi> I am never the nearer; <hi type="italic">what am I eased?</hi> If he complained he was censured as passionate; if not, as sullen. If he maintained his integrity, that was his crime; if he made no answer to their accusations, his silence was taken for a confession of his guilt. <div eID="gen9628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9629" type="x-p"/> Here is a doleful representation of Job's grievances. O what reason have we to bless God that we are not making such complaints! He complains, <div eID="gen9629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9630" type="x-p"/> I. That his family was scattered (<reference osisRef="Job.16.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He hath made me weary,</hi> weary of speaking, weary of forbearing, weary of my friends, weary of life itself; my journey through the world proves so very uncomfortable that I am quite tired with it." This made it as tiresome as any thing, that all his company was made desolate, his children and servants being killed and the poor remains of his great household dispersed. The company of good people that used to meet at his house for religious worship, was now scattered, and he spent his sabbaths in silence and solitude. He had company indeed, but such as he would rather have been without, for they seemed to triumph in his desolation. If lovers and friends are put far from us, we must see and own God's hand in it, making our company desolate. <div eID="gen9630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9631" type="x-p"/> II. That his body was worn away with diseases and pains, so that he had become a perfect skeleton, nothing but skin and bones, <reference osisRef="Job.16.8">v. 8</reference>. His face was furrowed, not with age, but sickness: <hi type="italic">Thou hast filled me with wrinkles.</hi> His flesh was wasted with the running of his sore boils, so that <hi type="italic">his leanness rose up in him,</hi> that is, his bones, that before were not seen, stuck out, <reference osisRef="Job.33.21">ch. xxxiii. 21</reference>. These are called <hi type="italic">witnesses against him,</hi> witnesses of God's displeasure against him, and such witnesses as his friends produced against him to prove him a wicked man. Or, "They are witnesses <hi type="italic">for</hi> me, that my complaint is not causeless," or "witnesses <hi type="italic">to</hi> me, that I am a dying man, and must be gone shortly." <div eID="gen9631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9632" type="x-p"/> III. That his enemy was a terror to him, threatened him, frightened him, looked sternly upon him, and gave all the indications of rage against him (<reference osisRef="Job.16.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">He tears me in his wrath.</hi> But who is this enemy? 1. Eliphaz, who showed himself very much exasperated against him, and perhaps had expressed himself with such marks of indignation as are here mentioned: at least, what he said tore Job's good name and thundered nothing but terror to him; his eyes were sharpened to spy out matter of reproach against Job, and very barbarously both he and the rest of them used him. Or, 2. Satan. He was his enemy that hated him, and perhaps, by the divine permission, terrified him with apparitions, as (some think) he terrified our Saviour, which put him into his agonies in the garden; and thus he aimed to make him curse God. It is not improbable that this is the enemy he means. Or, (3.) God himself. If we understand it of him, the expressions are indeed as rash as any he used. God hates none of his creatures; but Job's melancholy did thus represent to him the terrors of the Almighty: and nothing can be more grievous to a good man than to apprehend God to be his enemy. If the wrath of a king be as messengers of death, what is the wrath of the King of kings! <div eID="gen9632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9633" type="x-p"/> IV. That all about him were abusive to him, <reference osisRef="Job.16.10">v. 10</reference>. They came upon him with open mouth to devour him, as if they would swallow him alive, so terrible were their threats and so scornful was their conduct to him. They offered him all the indignities they could invent, and even smote him <hi type="italic">on the cheek;</hi> and herein many were confederate. <hi type="italic">They gathered themselves together against him,</hi> even the abjects, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.15">Ps. xxxv. 15</reference>. Herein Job was a type of Christ, as many of the ancients make him: these very expressions are used in the predictions of his sufferings, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.13">Ps. xxii. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">They gaped upon me with their mouths;</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Mic.5.1">Mic. v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">They shall smite the Judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek,</hi> which was literally fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.67">Matt. xxvi. 67</reference>. How were those increased that troubled him! <div eID="gen9633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9634" type="x-p"/> V. That God, instead of delivering him out of their hands, as he hoped, delivered him into their hands (<reference osisRef="Job.16.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">He hath turned me over into the hands of the wicked.</hi> They could have had no power against him if it had not been given them from above. He therefore looks beyond them to God who gave them their commission, as David did when Shimei cursed him; but he thinks it strange, and almost thinks it hard, that those should have power against him who were God's enemies as much as his. God sometimes makes use of wicked men as his sword to one another (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.13">Ps. xvii. 13</reference>) and his rod to his own children, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Isa. x. 5</reference>. Herein also Job was a type of Christ, who was delivered into wicked hands, to be crucified and slain, by the <hi type="italic">determinate counsel and fore-knowledge of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. <div eID="gen9634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9635" type="x-p"/> VI. That God not only delivered him into the hands of the wicked, but took him into his own hands too, into which it is a fearful thing to fall (<reference osisRef="Job.16.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I was at ease</hi> in the comfortable enjoyment of the gifts of God's bounty, not fretting and uneasy, as some are in the midst of their prosperity, who thereby provoke God to strip them; yet <hi type="italic">he has broken me asunder,</hi> put me upon the rack of pain, and torn me limb from limb." God, in afflicting him, had seemed, 1. As if he were furious. Though fury is not in God, he thought it was, when he took him <hi type="italic">by the neck</hi> (as a strong man in a passion would take a child) and shook him to pieces, triumphing in the irresistible power he had to do what he would with him. 2. As if he were partial. "He has distinguished me from the rest of mankind by this hard usage of me: <hi type="italic">He has set me up for his mark,</hi> the butt at which he is pleased to let fly all his arrows: at me they are directed, and they come not by chance; against me they are levelled, as if I were the greatest sinner of all the men of the east or were singled out to be made an example." When God set him up for a mark <hi type="italic">his archers</hi> presently <hi type="italic">compassed him round.</hi> God has archers at command, who will be sure to hit the mark that he sets up. Whoever are our enemies, we must look upon them as God's archers, and see him directing the arrow. <hi type="italic">It is the Lord; let him do what seemeth him good.</hi> 3. As if he were cruel, and his wrath as relentless as his power was resistless. As if he contrived to touch him in the tenderest part, <hi type="italic">cleaving his reins asunder</hi> with acute pains; perhaps they were nephritic pains, those of the stone, which lie in the region of the kidneys. As if he had no mercy in reserve for him, he does not spare nor abate any thing of the extremity. And as if he aimed at nothing but his death, and his death in the midst of the most grievous tortures: <hi type="italic">He pours out my gall upon the ground,</hi> as when men have taken a wild beast, and killed it, they open it, and pour out the gall with a loathing of it. He thought his blood was poured out, as if it were not only not precious, but nauseous. 4. As if he were unreasonable and insatiable in his executions (<reference osisRef="Job.16.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He breaketh me with breach upon breach,</hi> follows me with one wound after another." So his troubles came at first; while one messenger of evil tidings was speaking another came: and so it was still; new boils were rising every day, so that he had no prospect of the end of his troubles. Thus he thought that God ran upon him <hi type="italic">like a giant,</hi> whom he could not possibly stand before or confront; as the giants of old ran down all their poor neighbours, and were too hard for them. Note, Even good men, when they are in great and extraordinary troubles, have much ado not to entertain hard thoughts of God. <div eID="gen9635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9636" type="x-p"/> VII. That he had divested himself of all his honour, and all his comfort, in compliance with the afflicting providences that surrounded him. Some can lessen their own troubles by concealing them, holding their heads as high and putting on as good a face as ever; but Job could not do so: he received the impressions of them, and, as one truly penitent and truly patient, he humbled himself under the mighty hand of God, <reference osisRef="Job.16.15-Job.16.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. 1. He now laid aside all his ornaments and soft clothing, consulted not either his ease or finery in his dress, but sewed sackcloth upon his skin; that clothing he thought good enough for such a defiled distempered body as he had. Silks upon sores, such sores, he thought, would be unsuitable; sackcloth would be more becoming. Those are fond indeed of gay clothing that will not be weaned from it by sickness and old age, and, as Job was (<reference osisRef="Job.16.8">v. 8</reference>), by <hi type="italic">wrinkles and leanness.</hi> He not only put on sackcloth, but sewed it on, as one that resolved to continue his humiliation as long as the affliction continued. 2. He insisted not upon any points of honour, but humbled himself under humbling providences: <hi type="italic">He defiled his horn in the dust,</hi> and refused the respect that used to be paid to his dignity, power, and eminency. Note, When God brings down our condition, that should bring down our spirits. Better lay the horn in the dust than lift it up in contradiction to the designs of Providence and have it broken at last. Eliphaz had represented Job as high and haughty, and unhumbled under his affliction. "No," says Job, "I know better things; the dust is now the fittest place for me." 3. He banished mirth as utterly unseasonable, and set himself to sow in tears (<reference osisRef="Job.16.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My face is foul with weeping</hi> so constantly for my sins, for God's displeasure against me, and for my friends unkindness: this has brought a <hi type="italic">shadow of death upon my eyelids.</hi>" He had not only wept away all his beauty, but almost wept his eyes out. In this also he was a type of Christ, who was a man of sorrows, and much in tears, and pronounced those blessed that mourn, <hi type="italic">for they shall be comforted.</hi>
entries.298aae428119a203f6391457025364cd69897129: <div eID="gen9636" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Testimony of Conscience; Job's Comfort in Conscious Integrity. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9637" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Not for <hi type="italic">any</hi> injustice in mine hands: also my prayer <hi type="italic">is</hi> pure. <hi type="super">18</hi> O earth, cover not thou my blood, and let my cry have no place. <hi type="super">19</hi> Also now, behold, my witness <hi type="italic">is</hi> in heaven, and my record <hi type="italic">is</hi> on high. 20 My friends scorn me: <hi type="italic">but</hi> mine eye poureth out <hi type="italic">tears</hi> unto God. <hi type="super">21</hi> O that one might plead for a man with God, as a man <hi type="italic">pleadeth</hi> for his neighbour! <hi type="super">22</hi> When a few years are come, then I shall go the way <hi type="italic">whence</hi> I shall not return. <div eID="gen9637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9638" type="x-p"/> Job's condition was very deplorable; but had he nothing to support him, nothing to comfort him? Yes, and he here tells us what it was. <div eID="gen9638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9639" type="x-p"/> I. He had the testimony of his conscience for him that he had walked uprightly, and had never allowed himself in any gross sin. None was ever more ready than he to acknowledge his sins of infirmity; but, upon search, he could not charge himself with any enormous crime, for which he should be made more miserable than other men, <reference osisRef="Job.16.17">v. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen9639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9640" type="x-p"/> 1. He had kept a conscience void of offence, (1.) Towards men: "<hi type="italic">Not for any injustice in my hands,</hi> any wealth that I have unjustly got or kept." Eliphaz had represented him as a tyrant and an oppressor. "No," says he, "I never did any wrong to any man, but always despised the gain of oppression." (2.) Towards God: <hi type="italic">Also my prayer is pure;</hi> but prayer cannot be pure as long as there is <hi type="italic">injustice in our hands,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Isa. i. 15</reference>. Eliphaz had charged him with hypocrisy in religion, but he specifies prayer, the great act of religion, and professes that in that he was pure, though not from all infirmity, yet from reigning and allowed guile: it was not like the prayers of the Pharisees, who looked no further than to be seen of men, and to serve a turn. <div eID="gen9640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9641" type="x-p"/> 2. This assertion of his own integrity he backs with a solemn imprecation of shame and confusion to himself if it were not true, <reference osisRef="Job.16.18">v. 18</reference>. (1.) If there were any injustice in his hands, he wished it might not be concealed: <hi type="italic">O earth! cover thou not my blood,</hi> that is, "the innocent blood of others, which I am suspected to have shed." Murder will out; and "let it," says Job, "if I have ever been guilty if it," <reference osisRef="Gen.4.10-Gen.4.11">Gen. iv. 10, 11</reference>. The day is coming when <hi type="italic">the earth shall disclose her blood</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Isa. xxvi. 21</reference>), and a good man as far from dreading that day. (2.) If there were any impurity in his prayers, he wished they might not be accepted: <hi type="italic">Let my cry have no place.</hi> He was willing to be judged by that rule, <hi type="italic">If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">Ps. lxvi. 18</reference>. There is another probable sense of these words, that he does hereby, as it were, lay his death upon his friends, who broke his heart with their harsh censures, and charges the guilt of his blood upon them, begging of God to avenge it and that the cry of his blood might have no place in which to lie hid, but might come up to heaven and be heard by him that makes inquisition for blood. <div eID="gen9641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9642" type="x-p"/> II. He could appeal to God's omniscience concerning his integrity, <reference osisRef="Job.16.19">v. 19</reference>. The witness in our own bosoms for us will stand us in little stead if we have not a witness in heaven for us too; for <hi type="italic">God is greater than our hearts,</hi> and we are not to be our own judges. This therefore is Job's triumph, <hi type="italic">My witness is in heaven.</hi> Note, It is an unspeakable comfort to a good man, when he lies under the censure of his brethren, that there is a God in heaven who knows his integrity and will clear it up sooner or later. See <reference osisRef="John.5.31">John v. 31</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.37">37</reference>. This one witness is instead of a thousand. <div eID="gen9642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9643" type="x-p"/> III. He had a God to go to before whom he might unbosom himself, <reference osisRef="Job.16.20-Job.16.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. See here, 1. How the case stood between him and his friends. He knew not how to be free with them, nor could he expect either a fair hearing with them or fair dealing from them. "My friends (so they call themselves) scorn me; they set themselves not only to resist me, but to expose me; they are of counsel against me, and use all their art and eloquence" (so the word signifies) "to run me down." The scorns of friends are more cutting than those of enemies; but we must expect them, and provide accordingly. 2. How it stood between him and God. He doubted not but that, (1.) God did now take cognizance of his sorrows: <hi type="italic">My eye pours out tears to God.</hi> He had said (<reference osisRef="Job.16.16">v. 16</reference>) that he wept much; here he tells us in what channel his tears ran, and which way they were directed. His sorrow was not that of the world, but he sorrowed after a godly sort, wept before the Lord, and offered to him the sacrifice of a broken heart. Note, Even tears, when sanctified to God, give ease to troubled spirits; and, if men slight our grief, this may comfort us, that God regards them. (2.) That he would in due time clear up his innocency (<reference osisRef="Job.16.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">O that one might plead for a man with God!</hi> If he could but now have the same freedom at God's bar that men commonly have at the bar of the civil magistrate, he doubted not but to carry his cause, for the Judge himself was a witness to his integrity. The language of this wish is like that in <reference osisRef="Isa.50.7-Isa.50.8">Isa. l. 7, 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">I know that I shall not be ashamed, for he is near that justifies me.</hi> Some give a gospel sense of this verse, and the original will very well bear it; <hi type="italic">and he will plead</hi> (that is, there is one that will plead) <hi type="italic">for man with God, even the Son of man for his friend, or neighbour.</hi> Those who pour out tears before God, though they cannot plead for themselves, by reason of their distance and defects, have a friend to plead for them, even the Son of man, and on this we must bottom all our hopes of acceptance with God. <div eID="gen9643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9644" type="x-p"/> IV. He had a prospect of death which would put a period to all his troubles. Such confidence had he towards God that he could take pleasure in thinking of the approach of death, when he should be determined to his everlasting state, as one that doubted not but it would be well with him then: <hi type="italic">When a few years have come</hi> (<hi type="italic">the years of number</hi> which are determined and appointed to me) <hi type="italic">then I shall go the way whence I shall not return.</hi> Note, 1. To die is to <hi type="italic">go the way whence we shall not return.</hi> It is to go a journey, a long journey, a journey for good and all, to remove from this to another country, from the world of sense to the world of spirits. It is a journey to our long home; there will be no coming back to out state in this world nor any change of our state in the other world. 2. We must all of us very certainly, and very shortly, go this journey; and it is comfortable to those who keep a good conscience to think of it, for it is the crown of their integrity.  <chapter eID="Job.16"/> <div eID="gen9644" type="x-p"/>

entries.9bc37407eb2e96896580c420725adf89ba51cee9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4790"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <div sID="gen6977" type="x-p"/> SECOND SERIES.<div eID="gen6977" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.16.1-Job.16.22">Job 16:1-22</reference>. Job's Reply.</title> <div sID="gen6978" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4790"/>2. (<reference osisRef="Job.13.4">Job 13:4</reference>). <div eID="gen6978" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b2e575c2b58364d96fde5f0c1ec774f382ac8b8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4791"/><div sID="gen6979" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4791"/>3. "Words of wind," Hebrew. He retorts upon Eliphaz his reproach (<reference osisRef="Job.15.2">Job 15:2</reference>).<div eID="gen6979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">emboldeneth--</hi>literally, "What wearies you so that ye contradict?" that is, What have I said to provoke you? &c. [Schuttens]. Or, as better accords with the first clause, "Wherefore do ye weary yourselves contradicting?" [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen6980" type="x-p"/>
entries.2eacace3a04a6b4921c22d58afc1e825e6e58be3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4792"/><div sID="gen6981" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4792"/><hi type="bold">4. heap up--</hi>rather, "marshal together (an army of) words against you."<div eID="gen6981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6982" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shake ... head--</hi>in mockery; it means nodding, rather than shaking; nodding is not with us, as in the East, a gesture of scorn (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">Is 37:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.16">Jr 18:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.27.39">Mt 27:39</reference>). <div eID="gen6982" type="x-p"/>
entries.7cd82460e2f46cae3bba34afaae1a8f5bfc1d98e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4793"/><div sID="gen6983" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4793"/><hi type="bold">5. strengthen ... with ... mouth--</hi>bitter irony. In allusion to Eliphaz' boasted "consolations" (<reference osisRef="Job.15.11">Job 15:11</reference>). Opposed to strengthening with the heart, that is, with real consolation. Translate, "I also (like you) could strengthen with the mouth," that is, with heartless talk: "And the moving of my lips (mere lip comfort) could console (in the same fashion as you do)" [Umbreit]. "Hearty counsel" (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.9">Pr 27:9</reference>) is the opposite. <div eID="gen6983" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bbcecccd59211438d0e1ccd7af4fcdb149ba88f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4794"/><div sID="gen6984" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4794"/><hi type="bold">6. eased--</hi>literally, "What (portion of my sufferings) goes from me?" <div eID="gen6984" type="x-p"/>
entries.f2d27b285c0ebea134dce422207bc4c6b3232917: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4795"/><div sID="gen6985" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4795"/><hi type="bold">7. But now--</hi>rather, "ah!"<div eID="gen6985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6986" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>God.<div eID="gen6986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6987" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">company--</hi>rather, "band of witnesses," namely, those who could attest his innocence (his children, servants, &c.). So the same Hebrew is translated in <reference osisRef="Job.16.8">Job 16:8</reference>. Umbreit makes his "band of witnesses," himself, for, alas! he had no other witness for him. But this is too recondite. <div eID="gen6987" type="x-p"/>
entries.32b2e49509ee92375fd50d6292a9c79af5934377: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4796"/><div sID="gen6988" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4796"/><hi type="bold">8. filled ... with wrinkles--</hi>Rather (as also the same Hebrew word in <reference osisRef="Job.22.16">Job 22:16</reference>; English Version, "cut down"), "thou hast fettered me, thy witness" (besides cutting off my "band of witnesses," <reference osisRef="Job.16.7">Job 16:7</reference>), that is, hast disabled me by pains from properly attesting my innocence. But another "witness" arises against him, namely, his "leanness" or wretched state of body, construed by his friends into a proof of his guilt. The radical meaning of the Hebrew is "to draw together," whence flow the double meaning "to bind" or "fetter," and in Syriac, "to wrinkle."<div eID="gen6988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leanness--</hi>meaning also "lie"; implying it was a "false witness." <div eID="gen6989" type="x-p"/>
entries.e049af5f5d08e01fee1c0c40d80e6d2d4f1c0ef8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4797"/><div sID="gen6990" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4797"/>9. Image from a wild beast. So God is represented (<reference osisRef="Job.10.16">Job 10:16</reference>).<div eID="gen6990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6991" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who hateth me--</hi>rather, "and pursues me hard." Job would not ascribe "hatred" to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.22">Psa 50:22</reference>).<div eID="gen6991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6992" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mine enemy--</hi>rather, "he sharpens, &c., as an enemy" (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.12">Psa 7:12</reference>). Darts wrathful glances at me, like a foe (<reference osisRef="Job.13.24">Job 13:24</reference>). <div eID="gen6992" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac524a99d60c82549d967458c1644122432ac239: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4798"/><div sID="gen6993" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4798"/><hi type="bold">10. gaped--</hi>not in order to devour, but to mock him. To fill his cup of misery, the mockery of his friends (<reference osisRef="Job.16.10">Job 16:10</reference>) is added to the hostile treatment from God (<reference osisRef="Job.16.9">Job 16:9</reference>).<div eID="gen6993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6994" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smitten ... cheek--</hi>figurative for contemptuous abuse (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.30">La 3:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.39">Mt 5:39</reference>).<div eID="gen6994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6995" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gathered themselves--</hi>"conspired unanimously" [Schuttens]. <div eID="gen6995" type="x-p"/>
entries.22c182fb6863c06bdcae10149e0d7e708d26b793: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4799"/><div sID="gen6996" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4799"/><hi type="bold">11. the ungodly--</hi>namely, his professed friends, who persecuted him with unkind speeches.<div eID="gen6996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6997" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turned me over--</hi>literally, "cast me headlong into the hands of the wicked." <div eID="gen6997" type="x-p"/>
entries.5cf835580fc38af1a76f17105fb128d38bc1e588: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4800"/><div sID="gen6998" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4800"/><hi type="bold">12. I was at ease--</hi>in past times (<reference osisRef="Job.1.1-Job.1.3">Job 1:1-3</reference>).<div eID="gen6998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by my neck--</hi>as an animal does its prey (so <reference osisRef="Job.10.16">Job 10:16</reference>).<div eID="gen6999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7000" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shaken--</hi>violently; in contrast to his former "ease" (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.10">Psa 102:10</reference>). Set me up (again).<div eID="gen7000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7001" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mark--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.12">La 3:12</reference>). God lets me always recover strength, so as to torment me ceaselessly. <div eID="gen7001" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb6cb1150ad4d10bc3c1f27b71bb03a16cc2ea44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4801"/><div sID="gen7002" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4801"/><hi type="bold">13. his archers--</hi>The image of <reference osisRef="Job.16.12">Job 16:12</reference> is continued. God, in making me His "mark," is accompanied by the three friends, whose words wound like sharp arrows.<div eID="gen7002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gall--</hi>put for a vital part; so the liver (<reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">La 2:11</reference>). <div eID="gen7003" type="x-p"/>
entries.329b8fe7dab5924f002ea4a8ab5185bfc7d31cfc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4802"/><div sID="gen7004" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4802"/>14. The image is from storming a fortress by making breaches in the walls (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.13">2Ki 14:13</reference>).<div eID="gen7004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7005" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a giant--</hi>a mighty warrior. <div eID="gen7005" type="x-p"/>
entries.62a224b398160439913242ab465f57bdcba9e841: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4803"/><div sID="gen7006" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4803"/><hi type="bold">15. sewed--</hi>denoting the tight fit of the mourning garment; it was a sack with armholes closely sewed to the body.<div eID="gen7006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7007" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horn--</hi>image from horned cattle, which when excited tear the earth with their horns. The horn was the emblem of power (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.11">1Ki 22:11</reference>). Here, it is<div eID="gen7007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the dust--</hi>which as applied to Job denotes his humiliation from former greatness. To throw one's self in the dust was a sign of mourning; this idea is here joined with that of excited despair, depicted by the fury of a horned beast. The Druses of Lebanon still wear horns as an ornament. <div eID="gen7008" type="x-p"/>
entries.6cf55a4875c97e81ef62738b7a84802ce0e6d0e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4804"/><div sID="gen7009" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4804"/><hi type="bold">16. foul--</hi>rather, "is red," that is, flushed and heated [Umbreit and Noyes].<div eID="gen7009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shadow of death--</hi>that is, darkening through many tears (<reference osisRef="Lam.5.17">La 5:17</reference>). Job here refers to Zophar's implied charge (<reference osisRef="Job.11.14">Job 11:14</reference>). Nearly the same words occur as to Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">Is 53:9</reference>). So <reference osisRef="Job.16.10">Job 16:10</reference> above answers to the description of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.13">Psa 22:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Is 50:6</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Job.16.4">Job 16:4</reference> to <reference osisRef="Ps.22.7">Psa 22:7</reference>). He alone realized what Job aspired after, namely, outward righteousness of acts and inward purity of devotion. Jesus Christ as the representative man is typified in some degree in every servant of God in the Old Testament. <div eID="gen7010" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa7521bd2d901030e65b6e1148ead2e155b11099: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4805"/><div sID="gen7011" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4805"/><hi type="bold">18. my blood--</hi>that is, my undeserved suffering. He compares himself to one murdered, whose blood the earth refuses to drink up until he is avenged (<reference osisRef="Gen.4.10">Ge 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.4.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.1">Eze 24:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.8">8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Is 26:21</reference>). The Arabs say that the dew of heaven will not descend on a spot watered with innocent blood (compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.21">2Sa 1:21</reference>).<div eID="gen7011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7012" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no place--</hi>no resting-place. "May my cry never stop!" May it go abroad! "Earth" in this verse in antithesis to "heaven" (<reference osisRef="Job.16.19">Job 16:19</reference>). May my innocence be as well-known to man as it is even now to God! <div eID="gen7012" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6307cf73d29d9c46a92103248da5e470c28e639: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4806"/><div sID="gen7013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4806"/><hi type="bold">19. Also now--</hi>Even now, when I am so greatly misunderstood on earth, God in heaven is sensible of my innocence.<div eID="gen7013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">record--</hi>Hebrew, "in the high places"; Hebrew, "my witness." Amidst all his impatience, Job still trusts in God. <div eID="gen7014" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e18277e50593ef7fe40a81139fbcc3013e3116c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4807"/><div sID="gen7015" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4807"/><hi type="bold">20. Hebrew, "are my scorners"; more forcibly, "my mockers--</hi>my friends!" A heart-cutting paradox [Umbreit]. God alone remains to whom he can look for attestation of his innocence; plaintively with tearful eye, he supplicates for this. <div eID="gen7015" type="x-p"/>
entries.cabf8fcba39b8dacfd530e39c4f0c79b47a365cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4808"/><div sID="gen7016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4808"/><hi type="bold">21. one--</hi>rather, "He" (God). "Oh, that He would plead for a man (namely, me) against God." Job quaintly says, "God must support me against God; for He makes me to suffer, and He alone knows me to be innocent" [Umbreit]. So God helped Jacob in wrestling against Himself (compare <reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.32.25">Ge 32:25</reference>). God in Jesus Christ does plead with God for man (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Ro 8:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.27">27</reference>).<div eID="gen7016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a man--</hi>literally, "the Son of man." A prefiguring of the advocacy of Jesus Christ--a boon longed for by Job (<reference osisRef="Job.9.33">Job 9:33</reference>), though the spiritual pregnancy of his own words, designed for all ages, was but little understood by him (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.17">Psa 80:17</reference>).<div eID="gen7017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for his neighbour--</hi>Hebrew, "friend." Job himself (<reference osisRef="Job.42.8">Job 42:8</reference>) pleaded as intercessor for his "friends," though "his scorners" (<reference osisRef="Job.16.20">Job 16:20</reference>); so Jesus Christ the Son of man (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.34">Lu 23:34</reference>); "for friends" (<reference osisRef="John.15.13-John.15.15">Joh 15:13-15</reference>). <div eID="gen7018" type="x-p"/>
entries.b76ae4ae1ce1f50e6be0f690d38632ad00488363: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4809"/><div sID="gen7019" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4809"/><hi type="bold">22. few--</hi>literally, "years of number," that is, few, opposed to numberless (<reference osisRef="Gen.34.30">Ge 34:30</reference>). <chapter eID="Job.16"/>

entries.f7fa9a14db819f4cb836586a5871d877df2b671a: <div eID="gen16631" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16632" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16633" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16633" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16632" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16634" type="x-p"/> Job replies to Eliphaz, and through him to all his friends, who, instead of comforting him, had added to his misfortunes; and shows that, had they been in his circumstances, he would have treated them in a different manner, <reference osisRef="Job.16.1-Job.16.5">Job 16:1-5</reference>. Enters into an affecting detail of his suffering, <reference osisRef="Job.16.6-Job.16.16">Job 16:6-16</reference>. Consoles himself with the consciousness of his own innocence, of which he takes God to witness, and patiently expects a termination of all his sufferings by death, <reference osisRef="Job.16.17-Job.16.22">Job 16:17-22</reference>.
entries.e044fe7f5253b87b95152e0f931e03bfb6e244c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16635" type="x-p"/> I have heard many such things - These sayings of the ancients are not strange to me; but they do not apply to my case: ye see me in affliction; ye should endeavor to console me. This ye do not; and yet ye pretend to do it! Miserable comforters are ye all.
entries.738eb8a0586ca61589f711cbd7db6844069aa1ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16636" type="x-p"/> Vain words - Literally, words of air. <div eID="gen16636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16637" type="x-p"/> What emboldeneth thee - Thou art totally ignorant of the business; what then can induce thee to take part in this discussion?
entries.5d96c8b856e9c6743947f3872317bad9d3e15774: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16638" type="x-p"/> I also could speak - It is probably better to render some of these permissives or potential verbs literally in the future tense, as in the Hebrew: I also Will speak. Mr. Good has adopted this mode. <div eID="gen16638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16639" type="x-p"/> If your soul were in my soul's stead - If you were in my place, I also could quote many wise sayings that might tend to show that you were hypocrites and wicked men; but would this be fair? Even when I might not choose to go farther in assertion, I might shake my head by way of insinuation that there was much more behind, of which I did not choose to speak; but would this be right? That such sayings are in memory, is no proof that they were either made for me, or apply to my case.
entries.3650b096edfdee6ff0cf9307e8da0f3041a911c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16640" type="x-p"/> I would strengthen you with my mouth - Mr. Good translates thus: - "With my own mouth will I overpower you, <div eID="gen16640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16641" type="x-p"/> Till the quivering of my lips shall fail;" for which rendering he contends in his learned notes. This translation is countenanced by the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic versions.
entries.5f7361a5539f6802457dfba34d7abac5a67869cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16642" type="x-p"/> Though I speak - But it will be of no avail thus to speak; for reprehensions of your conduct will not serve to mitigate my sufferings.
entries.26900b6c90c7935b68b9a4414d685d53e0b42779: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16643" type="x-p"/> But now he hath made me weary - The Vulgate translates thus: - Nunc autem oppressit me dolor meus; et in nihilum redacti sunt omnes artus mei; "But now my grief oppresses me, and all my joints are reduced to nothing." Perhaps Job alluded here to his own afflictions, and the desolation of his family. Thou hast made me weary with continual affliction; my strength is quite exhausted; and thou hast made desolate all my company, not leaving me a single child to continue my name, or to comfort me in sickness or old age. Mr. Good translates: - "Here, indeed, hath he distracted me; <div eID="gen16643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16644" type="x-p"/> Thou hast struck apart all my witnesses."
entries.d8347b1a75ced61da1470f49ee05c3ef9d755fe0: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16645" type="x-p"/> Thou hast filled me with wrinkles - If Job's disease were the elephantiasis, in which the whole skin is wrinkled as the skin of the elephant, from which this species of leprosy has taken its name, these words would apply most forcibly to it; but the whole passage, through its obscurity, has been variously rendered. Calmet unites it with the preceding, and Houbigant is not very different. He translates thus: - "For my trouble hath now weakened all my frame, and brought wrinkles over me: he is present as a witness, and ariseth against me, who telleth lies concerning me; he openly contradicts me to my face." Mr. Good translates nearly in the same way; others still differently.
entries.3c072f3d7e295ef43748eaf498cef9d7c12c6c73: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16646" type="x-p"/> He teareth me in his wrath - Who the person is that is spoken of in this verse, and onward to the end of the fourteenth, has been a question on which commentators have greatly differed. Some think God, others Eliphaz, is intended: I think neither. Probably God permitted Satan to show himself to Job, and the horrible form which he and his demons assumed increased the misery under which Job had already suffered so much. All the expressions, from this to the end of the fourteenth verse, may be easily understood on this principle; e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.16.9">Job 16:9</reference> : "He (Satan) gnasheth upon me with his teeth; mine enemy sharpeneth his eyes upon me." <reference osisRef="Job.16.10">Job 16:10</reference> : "They (demons) have gaped on me with their mouth; - they have gathered themselves together against me." <reference osisRef="Job.16.11">Job 16:11</reference> : "God hath delivered me to the ungodly, (עויל avil, to the Evil One), and turned me over into the hands of the wicked." He hath abandoned me to be tortured by the tempter and his host. If we consider all these expressions as referring to Job's three friends, we must, in that case, acknowledge that the figures are all strained to an insufferable height, so as not to be justified by any figure of speech.
entries.9a31651e4ab35019134893ed046b20169cea17ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16647" type="x-p"/> His archers compass me - רביו rabbaiv "his great ones." The Vulgate and Septuagint translate this his spears; the Syriac, Arabic, and Chaldee, his arrows. On this and the following verse Mr. Heath observes: "The metaphor is here taken from huntsmen: first, they surround the beast; then he is shot dead; his entrails are next taken out; and then his body is broken up limb by limb."
entries.d092d3c0d6dea672a9b689620b076768a16816eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16648" type="x-p"/> I have sewed sackcloth - שק sak, a word that has passed into almost all languages, as I have already had occasion to notice in other parts of this work. <div eID="gen16648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16649" type="x-p"/> Defiled my horn in the dust - The horn was an emblem of power; and the metaphor was originally taken from beasts, such as the urus, wild ox, buffalo, or perhaps the rhinoceros, who were perceived to have so much power in their horns. Hence a horn was frequently worn on crowns and helmets, as is evident on ancient coins; and to this day it is an appendage to the diadem of the kings and chiefs of Abyssinia. In the second edition of Mr. Bruce's Travels in Abyssinia, vol. viii., plates 2 and 3, we have engravings of two chiefs, Kefla Yasous, and Woodage Ashahel, who are represented with this emblem of power on their forehead. Mr. Bruce thus describes it: "One thing remarkable in this cavalcade, which I observed, was the head dress of the governors of provinces. A large broad fillet was bound upon their forehead, and tied behind their head. In the middle of this was a horn, or a conical piece of silver, gilt, about four inches in length, much in the shape of our common candle extinguishers. This is called kirn, or horn; and is only worn in reviews, or parades after victory. This, I apprehend, like all others of their usages is taken from the Hebrews; and the several allusions made in Scripture to it arise from this practice. 'I said unto the fools, Deal not foolishly; and to the wicked, Lift not up the horn.' 'Lift not up your horn on high, speak not with a stiff neck; for promotion cometh not,' etc. 'But my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of a unicorn.' 'And the horn of the righteous shall be exalted with honor.' And so in many other places throughout the Psalms." In a note on the same page we have the following observation: "The crooked manner in which they hold their neck when this ornament is on their forehead, for fear it should fall forward, perfectly shows the meaning of 'Speak not with a stiff neck when you hold the horn on high (or erect) like the horn of the unicorn."' - Bruce's Travels, vol. iv., p. 407. Defiling or rolling the horn in the dust, signifies the disgrace or destruction of power, authority, and eminence. Mr. Good translates, I have rolled my turban in the dust, which he endeavors to justify in a long note. But in this, I think, this very learned man is mistaken. The Hebrew קרן keren is the same as the Ethiopic kirn, and both mean exactly, in such connection, what Mr. Bruce has noticed above. The horn on the diadem is the emblem of power, authority, and eminence.
entries.a027c5f2d7fe2759c6dc4697370b375e2d9aa745: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16650" type="x-p"/> On my eyelids is the shadow of death - Death is now fast approaching me; already his shadow is projected over me.
entries.7a2fd8604d8c172ce0443919f078ac45a12c757c: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen16650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16651" type="x-p"/> Not for any injustice - I must assert, even with my last breath, that the charges of my friends against me are groundless. I am afflicted unto death, but not on account of my iniquities. <div eID="gen16651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16652" type="x-p"/> Also my prayer is pure - I am no hypocrite, God knoweth.
entries.98d9f62a2c006eef6ab9a9ded404452f5fa01e41: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen16652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16653" type="x-p"/> O earth, cover not thou my blood - This is evidently an allusion to the murder of Abel, and the verse has been understood in two different ways: <div eID="gen16653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16654" type="x-p"/> 1. Job here calls for justice against his destroyers. His blood is his life, which he considers as taken away by violence, and therefore calls for vengeance. Let my blood cry against my murderers, as the blood of Abel cried against Cain. My innocent life is taken away by violence, as his innocent life was; as therefore the earth was not permitted to cover his blood, so that his murderer should be concealed, let my death be avenged in the same way. <div eID="gen16654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16655" type="x-p"/> 2. It has been supposed that the passage means that Job considered himself accused of shedding innocent blood; and, conscious of his own perfect innocence, he prays that the earth may not cover any blood shed by him. Thus Mr. Scott: - "O earth, the blood accusing me reveal; <div eID="gen16655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16656" type="x-p"/> Its piercing voice in no recess conceal." <div eID="gen16656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16657" type="x-p"/> And this notion is followed by Mr. Good. But, with all deference to these learned men, I do not see that this meaning can be supported by the Hebrew text; nor was the passage so understood by any of the ancient versions. I therefore prefer the first sense, which is sufficiently natural, and quite in the manner of Job in his impassioned querulousness.
entries.5976363015fd6b347a18c236079e969ea4503f90: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen16657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16658" type="x-p"/> My witness is in heaven - I appeal to God for my innocence.
entries.20769a3cce8dcb1a3b13eb9d8173f127d3005fd4: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16659" type="x-p"/> My friends scorn me - They deride and insult me, but my eye is towards God; I look to him to vindicate my cause.
entries.88e8ac3eca8ebc0b52344036573f1084b549e060: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16660" type="x-p"/> O that one might plead - Let me only have liberty to plead with God, as a man hath with his fellow.
entries.8a8949ad0de1027e75aacce1cc52b6db42db7693: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16661" type="x-p"/> When a few years are come - I prefer Mr. Good's version: - "But the years numbered to me are come. <div eID="gen16661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16662" type="x-p"/> And I must go the way whence I shall not return." <div eID="gen16662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16663" type="x-p"/> Job could not, in his present circumstances, expect a few years of longer life; from his own conviction he was expecting death every hour. The next verse, the first of the following chapter, should come in here: <div eID="gen16663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16664" type="x-p"/> My breath is corrupt, etc. - He felt himself as in the arms of death: he saw the grave as already digged which was to receive his dead body. This verse shows that our translation of the twenty-second verse is improper, and vindicates Mr. Good's version. <div eID="gen16664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16665" type="x-p"/> I Have said on <reference osisRef="Job.16.9">Job 16:9</reference> that a part of Job's sufferings probably arose from appalling representations made to his eye or to his imagination by Satan and his agents. I think this neither irrational nor improbable. That he and his demons have power to make themselves manifest on especial occasions, has been credited in all ages of the world; not by the weak, credulous, and superstitious only, but also by the wisest, the most learned, and the best of men. I am persuaded that many passages in the Book of Job refer to this, and admit of an easy interpretation on this ground.  <chapter eID="Job.16"/> <div eID="gen16665" type="x-p"/>

entries.e13b7741dd665747e342c54ff08eb19d24550a0d: <reference osisRef="Job.16.1-Job.5.1">Job 16:1-5   1</reference>  Then began Job, and said:   2  I have now heard such things in abundance, <div eID="gen7519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7520" type="x-p"/> Troublesome comforters are ye all!   3  Are windy words now at an end, <div eID="gen7520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7521" type="x-p"/> Or what goadeth thee that thou answerest?   4  I also would speak like you, <div eID="gen7521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7522" type="x-p"/> If only your soul were in my soul’s stead. <div eID="gen7522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7523" type="x-p"/> I would weave words against you, <div eID="gen7523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7524" type="x-p"/> And shake my head at you;   5  I would encourage you with my mouth, <div eID="gen7524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7525" type="x-p"/> And the solace of my lips should soothe you. <div eID="gen7525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7526" type="x-p"/> The speech of Eliphaz, as of the other two, is meant to be comforting. It is, however, primarily an accusation; it wounds instead of soothing. Of this kind of speech, says Job, one has now heard רבּות, much, i.e., (in a pregnant sense) amply sufficient, although the word might signify elliptically (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.43">Psa 106:43</reference>; comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.9.28">Neh 9:28</reference>) many times (Jer. <hi type="italic">frequenter</hi>); <hi type="italic">multa</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Job.23.14">Job 23:14</reference>) is, however, equally suitable, and therefore is to be preferred as the more natural. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.16.2">Job 16:2</reference></hi> shows how כּאלּה is intended; they are altogether עמל מנחמי, <hi type="italic">consolatores onerosi</hi> (Jer.), such as, instead of alleviating, only cause עמל, <hi type="italic">molestiam</hi> (comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.13.4">Job 13:4</reference>). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.16.3">Job 16:3</reference></hi> Job returns their reproach of being windy, i.e., one without any purpose and substance, which they brought against him, Job 15:2.: have windy words an end, or (לו <hi type="italic">vel</hi>  = אם in a disjunctive question, Ges. §155, 2, <hi type="italic">b</hi>) if not, what goads thee on to reply? מרץ has been already discussed on Job 6:25. The Targ. takes it in the sense of מלץ: what makes it sweet to thee, etc.; the Jewish interpreters give it, without any proof, the signification, to be strong; the lxx transl. παρενοχλήσει, which is not transparent. Hirz., Ew., Schlottm., and others, call in the help of the Arabic <hi type="italic">marida</hi> (Aramaic מרע), to be sick, the IV. form of which signifies “to make sick,” not “to injure.”<note placement="foot">The primary meaning of Arabic <hi type="italic">marida</hi> (root <hi type="italic">mr, stringere</hi>) is <hi type="italic">maceratum esse</hi>, by pressing, rubbing, beating, to be tender, enervated (Germ. dialectic and popul. <hi type="italic">abmaracht</hi>); comp. the nearest related <hi type="italic">maratsa</hi>, then <hi type="italic">maraza</hi>, <hi type="italic">marasa</hi>, <hi type="italic">maraa</hi>, and further, the development of the meaning of <hi type="italic">morbus</hi> and μαλαακία; - originally and first, of bodily sickness, then also of diseased affections and conditions of spirit, as envy, hatred, malice, etc.; vid., <hi type="italic">Sur</hi>. 2, v. 9, and Beidhâwi thereon. - Fl.</note> <div eID="gen7526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7527" type="x-p"/> We keep to the primary meaning, to pierce, penetrate; <hi type="italic">Hiph.</hi> to goad, bring out, <hi type="italic">lacessere:</hi> what incites thee, that (כי as <reference osisRef="Job.6.11">Job 6:11</reference>, <hi type="italic">quod</hi> not <hi type="italic">quum</hi>) thou repliest again? The collective thought of what follows is not that he also, if they were in his place, could do as they have done; that he, however, would not so act (thus e.g., Blumenfeld: with reasons for comfort I would overwhelm you, and sympathizingly shake my head over you, etc.). This rendering is destroyed by the shaking of the head, which is never a gesture of pure compassion, but always of malignant joy, Sir. 12:18; or of mockery at another’s fall, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.22">Isa 37:22</reference>; and misfortune, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.8">Psa 22:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.16">Jer 18:16</reference>; Mat 27:39. Hence Merc. considers the antithesis to begin with <reference osisRef="Job.16.5">Job 16:5</reference>, where, however, there is nothing to indicate it: <hi type="italic">minime id facerem, quin potius vos confirmarem ore meo</hi> - rather: that he also could display the same miserable consolation; he represents to them a change of their respective positions, in order that, as in a mirror, they may recognise the hatefulness of their conduct. The negative antecedent clause <hi type="italic">si essem</hi> (with לוּ, according to Ges. §155, 2, <hi type="italic">f</hi>) is surrounded by cohortatives, which (since the interrogative form of interpretation is inadmissible) signify not only <hi type="italic">loquerer,</hi> but <hi type="italic">loqui possem,</hi> or rather <hi type="italic">loqui vellem</hi> (comp. e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.51.18">Psa 51:18</reference>, <hi type="italic">dare vellem</hi>). When he says: I would range together, etc. (Carey: I would combine), he gives them to understand that their speeches are more artificial than natural, more declamations than the outgushings of the heart; instead of מלּים, it is בּמלּים, since the object of the action is thought is as the means, as in <reference osisRef="Job.16.4">Job 16:4</reference> ראשׁי במּו, <hi type="italic">capite meo</hi> (for <hi type="italic">caput meum</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.8">Psa 22:8</reference>), and בּפיהם, <reference osisRef="Job.16.10">Job 16:10</reference>, for פּיּהם, comp. <reference osisRef="Jer.18.16">Jer 18:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.1.17">Lam 1:17</reference>, Ges. §138† ; Ew. takes חהביר by comparison of the Arabic <hi type="italic">chbr</hi>, to know (the IV. form of which, <hi type="italic">achbara ,</hi> however, signifies to cause to know, announce), in a sense that belongs neither to the Heb. nor to the Arab.: to affect wisdom. In <reference osisRef="Job.16.5">Job 16:5</reference> the chief stress is upon “with my mouth,” without the heart being there, so also on the word “my lips,” solace (ניד ἅπ. λεγ., recalling <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Isa 57:19</reference>, ניב שׂפתים, offspring or fruit of the lips) of my lips, i.e., dwelling only on the lips, and not coming from the heart. In ''אאמּצכם (<hi type="italic">Piel,</hi> not <hi type="italic">Hiph.</hi>) the <hi type="italic">Ssere</hi> is shortened to <hi type="italic">Chirek</hi> (Ges. §60, rem. 4). According to <reference osisRef="Job.16.6">Job 16:6</reference>, כאבכם is to be supplied to יחשׂך. He also could offer such superficial condolence without the sympathy which places itself in the condition and mood of the sufferer, and desires to afford that relief which it cannot. And yet how urgently did he need right and effectual consolation! He is not able to console himself, as the next strophe says: neither by words nor by silence is his pain assuaged.
entries.9d0f76f3714076a20ed80765f6308b3bdbf38721: <reference osisRef="Job.16.6-Job.9.6">Job 16:6-9   6</reference>  If I speak, my pain is not soothed; <div eID="gen7527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7528" type="x-p"/> And if I forbear, what alleviation do I experience?   7  Nevertheless now hath He exhausted me; <div eID="gen7528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7529" type="x-p"/> Thou hast desolated all my household,   8  And Thou filledst me with wrinkles - for a witness was it, <div eID="gen7529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7530" type="x-p"/> And my leanness rose up against me <div eID="gen7530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7531" type="x-p"/> Complaining to my face.   9  His wrath tore me, and made war upon me; <div eID="gen7531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7532" type="x-p"/> He hath gnashed upon me with His teeth, <div eID="gen7532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7533" type="x-p"/> As mine enemy He sharpeneth His eyes against me. אם stands with the cohortative in the hypothetical antecedent clause <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.16.6">Job 16:6</reference></hi>, and in 6 <hi type="italic">b </hi>the cohortative stands alone as <reference osisRef="Job.11.17">Job 11:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.73.16">Psa 73:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.8">Psa 139:8</reference>, which is more usual, and more in accordance with the meaning which the cohortative has in itself, Nägelsbach, §89, 3. The interrogative, What goes from me? is equivalent to, what (= nothing) of pain forsakes me. The subject of the assertion which follows (<reference osisRef="Job.16.7">Job 16:7</reference>) is not the pain - Aben-Ezra thinks even that this is addressed in v. 7 <hi type="italic">b - </hi>still less Eliphaz, whom some think, particularly on account of the sharp expressions which follow, must be understood, but God, whose wrath Job regards as the cause of his suffering, and feels as the most intolerable part of it. A strained connection is obtained by taking אך either in an affirmative sense (Ew.: surely), as <reference osisRef="Job.18.21">Job 18:21</reference>, or in a restrictive sense: only (= entirely) He has now exhausted me (Hirz., Hahn, also Schlottm.: only I feel myself oppressed, at least to express this), by which interpretation the עתּה, which stands between אך and the verb, is in the way. We render it therefore in the adversative signification: nevertheless (<hi type="italic">verum tamen</hi>) now he seeks neither by speaking to alleviate his pain, nor by silence to control himself; God has placed him in a condition in which all his strength is exhausted. He is absolutely incapable of offering any resistance to his pain, and care has also been taken that no solacing word shall come to him from any quarter: Thou hast made all my society desolate (Carey: all my clan); עדה of the household, as in Job 15:34. Jerome: <hi type="italic">in nihilum redacti sunt omnes artus mei</hi> (כל אברי, as explained by the Jewish expositors, e.g., Ralbag), as though the human organism could be called עדה. Hahn: Thou hast destroyed all my testimony, which must have been אדתי (from עוּד, whereas עדה, from ועד, has a changeable <hi type="italic">Ssere</hi>). He means to say that he stands entirely alone, and neither sees nor hears anything consolatory, for he does not count his wife. He is therefore completely shut up to himself; God has shrivelled him up; and this suffering form to which God has reduced him, is become an evidence, i.e., for himself and for others, as the three friends, an accusation <hi type="italic">de facto</hi>, which puts him down as a sinner, although his self-consciousness testifies the opposite to him.
entries.35c8351bfe0cfe4e25310f0d496a8efa8e05c88d: <reference osisRef="Job.16.10-Job.11.10">Job 16:10-11 10</reference>  They have gaped against me with their mouth, <div eID="gen7534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7535" type="x-p"/> In contempt they smite my cheeks; <div eID="gen7535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7536" type="x-p"/> They conspire together against me. 11  God left me to the mercy of the ungodly, <div eID="gen7536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7537" type="x-p"/> And cast me into the hands of the evil-doer. <div eID="gen7537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7538" type="x-p"/> He does not mean the friends by those who mock and vex him with their contemptuous words, but the men around him who envied his prosperity and now rejoice at his misfortune; those to whom his uprightness was a burden, and who now consider themselves disencumbered of their liege lord, the over-righteous, censorious, godly man. The perfects here also have not a present signification; he depicts his suffering according to the change it has wrought since it came upon him. The verb פּער is used with the instrumental <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> instead of with the acc., as <reference osisRef="Job.29.23">Job 29:23</reference> (comp. on במלים, <reference osisRef="Job.16.4">Job 16:4</reference>): they make an opening with their mouth (similar to <reference osisRef="Ps.22.8">Psa 22:8</reference>, they make an opening with the lips, for <hi type="italic">diducunt labia</hi>). Smiting on the cheeks is in itself an insult (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.30">Lam 3:30</reference>); the additional בּחרפּה will therefore refer to insulting words which accompany the act. The <hi type="italic">Hithpa.</hi> התמלּא, which occurs only here, signifies not only to gather together a מלא in general, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.4">Isa 31:4</reference>, but (after the Arab. <hi type="italic">tamâla'a ‛ala</hi>, to conspire against any one)<note placement="foot">Wetzstein thinks the signification <hi type="italic">conspirare</hi> for יתמלאון poor in this connection, and prefers to translate: All together <hi type="italic">they eat themselves full</hi> upon me, התמלּא as reflexive of מלּא, <reference osisRef="Job.38.39">Job 38:39</reference>, synon. of נשׂבע, as in “the Lovers of <hi type="italic">Amâsiâ</hi>,” <hi type="italic">Ferhhât</hi>, after the death of his beloved, cries out: We are not separated! To-morrow (i.e., soon) the All-kind One will unite us in paradise, and we shall satisfy ourselves one with another (Arab. <hi type="italic">w-ntmll' mn b-'dnâ 'l-b'd</hi>). One would, however, expect ממּנּי instead of עלי; but perhaps we may refer to the interchange of התענג על, <reference osisRef="Job.22.26">Job 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.10">Job 27:10</reference>, with התענג מן, Isa 66:11.</note> to complete one’s self, to strengthen one’s self (for a like hostile purpose): Reiske correctly: <hi type="italic">sibi invicem mutuam et auxiliatricem operam contra me simul omnes ferunt.</hi><note placement="foot">The signification to <hi type="italic">help</hi>, which belongs to the I. form Arab. <hi type="italic">mala'a</hi>, proceeds from <hi type="italic">malâ'un</hi>, to have abundance, to be well off; prop. to be able to furnish any one with the means (<hi type="italic">opes, copias</hi>) for anything, and thereby to place him in a position to accomplish it. Comp. the Lat. <hi type="italic">ops, opem ferre, opitulari, opes, opulentus</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">malâ'un</hi>). - Fl.</note> <div eID="gen7538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7539" type="x-p"/> The meaning of עויל is manifest from <reference osisRef="Job.21.11">Job 21:11</reference>; from עוּל, to suckle, <hi type="italic">alere</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">‛âl med . Wau ,</hi> whence the inf. <hi type="italic">‛aul , ‛uwûl ,</hi> and <hi type="italic">‛ijâle</hi>), it signifies boys, knaves; and it is as unnecessary to suppose two forms, עויל and עויל, as two meanings, <hi type="italic">puer</hi> and <hi type="italic">pravus</hi>, since the language and particularly the book of Job has coined עוּל for the latter signification: it signifies in all three passages (here and <reference osisRef="Job.19.18">Job 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.11">Job 21:11</reference>) boys, or the boyish, childish, knavish. The Arabic <hi type="italic">warratta</hi> leaves no doubt as to the derivation and meaning of ירטני; it signifies to cast down to destruction (<hi type="italic">warttah</hi>, a precipice, ruin, danger), and so here the <hi type="italic">fut. Kal</hi> ירטני for יירטני (Ges. §69, rem. 3), <hi type="italic">praecipitem me dabat</hi> (lxx ἔῤῥιψε, Symm. ἐνέβαλε), as the <hi type="italic">praet. Kal,</hi> Num 22:32 : <hi type="italic">praeceps</hi> = <hi type="italic">exitiosa est via</hi>. The preformative <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> has <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> in correct texts, so that we need not suppose, with Ralbag, a רטה, similar in meaning to ירט.
entries.6148dd57a0e6574e9240ef2890236df51b581d7f: <reference osisRef="Job.16.12-Job.14.12">Job 16:12-14 12</reference>  I was at ease, but He hath broken me in pieces; <div eID="gen7539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7540" type="x-p"/> And He hath taken me by the neck and shaken me to pieces, <div eID="gen7540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7541" type="x-p"/> And set me up for a mark for himself. 13  His arrows whistled about me; <div eID="gen7541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7542" type="x-p"/> He pierced my reins without sparing; <div eID="gen7542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7543" type="x-p"/> He poured out my gall upon the ground. 14  He brake through me breach upon breach, <div eID="gen7543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7544" type="x-p"/> He ran upon me like a mighty warrior. <div eID="gen7544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7545" type="x-p"/> He was prosperous and contented, when all at once God began to be enraged against him; the intensive form פּרפּר (Arab. <hi type="italic">farfara</hi>) signifies to break up entirely, crush, crumble in pieces (<hi type="italic">Hithpo.</hi> to become fragile, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.19">Isa 24:19</reference>); the corresponding intensive form פּצפּץ (from פּצץ, Arab. <hi type="italic">fḍḍ</hi>, cogn. נפץ), to beat in pieces (<hi type="italic">Polel</hi> of a hammer, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.29">Jer 23:29</reference>), to dash to pieces: taking him by the neck, God raised him on high in order to dash him to the ground with all His might. מטּרה (from נטר, τηρεῖν, like σκοπός from σκέπτισθαι) is the target, as in the similar passage, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.12">Lam 3:12</reference>, distinct from מפגּע, <reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>, object of attack and point of attack: God has set me up for a target for himself, in order as it were to try what He and His arrows can do. Accordingly רבּיו (from רבב = רבה, רמה, <hi type="italic">jacere</hi>) signifies not: His archers (although this figure would be admissible after <reference osisRef="Job.10.17">Job 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.12">Job 19:12</reference>, and the form after the analogy of רב, רע, etc., is naturally taken as a substantival adj.), but, especially since God appears directly as the actor: His arrows (= הצּיו, <reference osisRef="Job.6.4">Job 6:4</reference>), from רב, formed after the analogy of בּז, מס, etc., according to which it is translated by lxx, Targ., Jer., while most of the Jewish expositors, referring to <reference osisRef="Jer.50.29">Jer 50:29</reference> (where we need not, with Böttch., point רבים, and here רביו), interpret by מורי החצים. On all sides, whichever way he might turn himself, the arrows of God flew about him, mercilessly piercing his reins, so that his gall-bladder became empty (comp. <reference osisRef="Lam.2.11">Lam 2:11</reference>, and vid., <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 268). It is difficult to conceive what is here said;<note placement="foot">The emptying of the gall takes place if the gall-bladder or any of its ducts are torn; but how the gall itself (without assuming some morbid condition) can flow outwardly, even with a severe wound, is a difficult question, with which only those who have no appreciation of the standpoint of imagery and poetry will distress themselves.
